To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV positive mothers in Ethiopia are faced with a dilemma of breastfeeding and that the fear of breast milk is out of proportion to the evidence of the risk of HIV.
the risk of HIV infection through breastfeeding is a new and challenging issue that has been interpreted as a risk to the child, the mother and society as a whole.

HIV positive mothers in Ethiopia have developed a fear of breast milk, which is out of proportions compared to the documented evidence of the risk of HIV infection through breast milk, and that the fear has also spread to health professionals in PMTCT services.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the HIV epidemic has affected breastfeeding and the meaning of breastfeeding for HIV positive mothers and health professionals in Addis Aboba, Ethiopia.
the meaning of breastfeeding for HIV positive mothers and the way in which HIV has affected the breastfeeding culture in Ethiopia.
the meaning of breastfeeding in HIV positive mothers in a context of HIV/AIDS, where breastfeeding is a contested practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV epidemic is a threat to breastfeeding, and that this threat has to be taken seriously.
the fear of breast milk is not justified and that the fear of formula milk is more than justified.
the fear of breast milk is not justified by the evidence of risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV epidemic has brought to light a paradoxical situation where the health benefits of breastfeeding are undermined by a new and intense fear of HIV positive mothers breast milk.
the HIV epidemic has changed the meaning of breastfeeding for HIV positive mothers, from being a source of life to a source of poison and sin.
the HIV epidemic has created new fears about the safety of breast milk.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a need for more public health education to promote exclusive breastfeeding among all mothers, including HIV positive mothers, and that there is a great risk of infant morbidity when infants are not breastfed.
the HIV epidemic has brought about new meanings to breastfeeding and infant feeding in general, which need to be taken into account in future research and public health programs.

there is a strong need for a public health response to the fear and anxiety of HIV positive mothers' breast milk, and for a public health approach to breastfeeding that is not based on the HIV epidemic.
